explanations.answer: A great number of Jews and Greeks believe
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Verse 1 says they spoke so well that “…a great number of Jews and Greeks believed.” Not a few. A GREAT number. I've baked batches where three people showed up for cookies, so this one has me jealous.

explanations.answer: The leaders ask them to preach every Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Nice idea, but the text doesn't mention any invitation like that. What it says is that they spoke so well that “…a great number of Jews and Greeks believed.” The big result is people believing, and that's the part to remember. A regular speaking slot would have been a nice bonus, but nobody wrote it down.

explanations.answer: The rulers invite them to speak at the palace
explanations.explanation: No palace in this passage, friend. The rulers do show up in verse 5, but not with an invitation. Together with the Gentiles and Jews, they set out to mistreat and stone Paul and Barnabas. That is a very different kind of guest list.

I see why you'd think so, because that's what most of us would do. But verse 3 says Paul and Barnabas “…spent considerable time there, speaking boldly for the Lord…” They didn't dash out the back door. They stayed and kept talking, and that takes some nerve.

False is right, friend. Verse 3 says they “…spent considerable time there, speaking boldly for the Lord…” Minds were getting poisoned, and these two stayed put and kept speaking. If somebody was bad-mouthing my cookies around town, I'd be hiding under the counter.

explanations.answer: He enables them to perform signs and wonders
explanations.explanation: You got it. Verse 3 says the Lord “…affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.” The credit goes to Him, not to the two men. Paul and Barnabas carried the message, and the Lord backed it up.

explanations.answer: He sends an angel to stand guard beside them
explanations.explanation: An angel has a nice ring to it, but this passage doesn't mention one in Iconium. Verse 3 says the Lord affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders. So the backup came through what Paul and Barnabas were enabled to do. Friend, I can't add an angel to a text that doesn't have one.

explanations.answer: He makes the city rulers protect them
explanations.explanation: The rulers go the other direction. In verse 5, the Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, set out to mistreat and stone Paul and Barnabas. The backup in verse 3 is that the Lord enabled them to perform signs and wonders. Protection from the rulers is nowhere in the text.

That's the one. Verse 6 says they found out about the plan and fled to “…the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe…” They also went to the surrounding region. When you hear about a stoning plan, you pack fast.

Good try, but verse 6 names a different pair of towns. They fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region. Tarsus and Joppa don't show up in this passage. Next time I'm reading the map before I pack my apron.

Salamis and Paphos have a great ring to them, but they're not on this map. Verse 6 says they fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region. Those two towns are where the story goes next. I'd have picked a pair by how good the names sound too, friend.

That's right, friend. Verse 7 says that in Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding region, “…they continued to preach the gospel.” Run out of one town, and they keep right on preaching in the next. That's not a quitter's schedule.

I get it, after fleeing for their lives you'd expect a break. But verse 7 says that in Lystra and Derbe and the region around them, “…they continued to preach the gospel.” They kept going. Nothing in the text shows them stopping.
Yes, faith. Verse 9 says Paul looked intently at the man and “…saw that he had faith to be healed.” The man was listening to Paul's words when that happened. I think those words stuck in his heart.
Strength sounds reasonable for a man who has never walked. But verse 9 says Paul saw that he had faith to be healed. The man was listening to Paul's words, and that's the word the text uses.
Courage would be a good guess, and I'd give this man plenty of it. But verse 9 says Paul looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed. Faith is the word in the text, friend.

explanations.answer: He jumps up and begins to walk
explanations.explanation: That's what verse 10 says: “And the man jumped up and began to walk.” This man had been lame from birth and had never walked. JUMPED. Not crept, not wobbled. Jumped.

explanations.answer: He stands but cannot take a step
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd picture a slow start. But verse 10 says the man “…jumped up and began to walk.” There's no stumbling and no wobbling in the text. He had never walked, and he jumped to his feet.

explanations.answer: He asks Paul to pray for him first
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show the man asking for anything. Paul calls out in a loud voice, “Stand up on your feet!” and the man jumped up and began to walk. Verse 9 says he was listening to Paul's words. Paul called, and the man answered with his feet.
Yes, friend. Verse 12 says they called Barnabas Zeus, a Greek god. The priest of Zeus even had a temple just outside the city (verse 13). That's a big promotion for a traveling preacher.
Baal was a false god too, one Israel kept falling for (Judges 2:13). But verse 12 says the crowd in Lystra called Barnabas Zeus. Baal isn't named in this passage.
Dagon was a god the Philistines worshiped (1 Samuel 5:2), so it's a clever pick. But verse 12 says they called Barnabas Zeus. Dagon doesn't appear in Lystra at all. Different crowd, different god.
That's right. Verse 12 says they called Paul Hermes “…because he was the chief speaker.” So the crowd named him for his talking. I've been called plenty for talking too much, but never Hermes.
Builder sounds like a solid job title, friend, but it's not the word here. Verse 12 says they called Paul Hermes because he was the chief speaker. The crowd was reacting to who did the talking.
These two had put on plenty of miles, so traveler makes sense. But verse 12 says the crowd called Paul Hermes because he was the chief speaker. It was the talking that got his name picked.

explanations.answer: Offer a sacrifice along with the crowds
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 13 says the priest brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, “…hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds.” This was a real plan, with real bulls. Bulls and wreaths at the city gates means somebody was serious.

explanations.answer: Crown Paul and Barnabas as kings
explanations.explanation: Wreaths might make you think of a crown, but the text says kings nowhere. Verse 13 says the priest of Zeus brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds. It's a sacrifice, not a coronation.

explanations.answer: Lead a parade through the whole city
explanations.explanation: A parade would use a lot of wreaths, I'll give you that. But verse 13 says the priest brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, “…hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds.” No parade route is in the text.

That's right, friend. Verse 14 says when the apostles Barnabas and Paul found out, “…they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting…” They tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd. That's the text's own picture.
This one is True, friend. Verse 14 says when Barnabas and Paul found out, “…they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting…” They did not sit this one out.

That's the word. Verse 15 says to “…turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them.” They set the worthless things next to the living God. That's a very short list of choices.
Old things can be good, so ancient doesn't land the point. Verse 15 says they were to turn from these “worthless things.” The text names them worthless, not ancient.

I see the thinking, but foreign isn't what the text says. Verse 15 tells the crowd to turn from these worthless things to the living God. It's about what the things are worth, not where they come from.

explanations.answer: Rain from heaven and fruitful seasons
explanations.explanation: You got it. Verse 17 says, “He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.” That's the testimony they point to. Rain on the field, food on the table, gladness in the heart.

explanations.answer: Stars that light up the night sky
explanations.explanation: I love stars, my own night sky is full of them. But verse 17 doesn't name them. It says God gives “…rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.” Paul and Barnabas pointed to the rain and the seasons.

Rivers are a good guess, but they're not in the text. Verse 17 says He gives “…rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.” Nothing about rivers, and nothing about them never running dry.

I wish it were that easy, friend. But verse 18 says that even with these words, Paul and Barnabas “…could hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them.” Hardly stop. The crowds were NOT calming down easily.

False is right. Verse 18 says even with these words, Paul and Barnabas “…could hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them.” They gave their whole speech and it was still a struggle. That's a tough crowd.
Yes. Verse 19 says they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, “…presuming he was dead.” This is a heavy moment, and I think it hurts to read. I'll stay quiet here and let the verse say it.

Verse 19 says otherwise. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, “…presuming he was dead.” That's what the people thought. It's a heavy part of the story, and I think it deserves a quiet moment.

explanations.answer: Gets up and goes back into the city
explanations.explanation: That's what verse 20 says. After the disciples gathered around him, “…he got up and went back into the city.” The next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. I think those disciples had a lot of feelings in that moment.

explanations.answer: Asks them to carry him to Derbe
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show Paul asking to be carried. Verse 20 says he got up and went back into the city, and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. Paul and Barnabas made that trip together.

explanations.answer: Rests outside the city for a week
explanations.explanation: A week of rest would sound reasonable to me. But verse 20 says Paul got up and went back into the city, and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. The text has him leaving the next day, not after a week.
Yes. Verse 21 says they preached the gospel to that city and “…made many disciples.” After all they'd been through, this is good news. Many disciples in Derbe, friend.
Getting driven out would be a rough ending, but verse 21 says something different about Derbe. They preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. No chase scene here.
The text says the opposite. Verse 21 says they preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. I'd call that a full house, friend.

It would be a safe plan, but they didn't take it. Verse 21 says that after Derbe, they “…returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch…” Those are the same towns where Paul was stoned and where a stoning plan started. They returned to them anyway.
False is right. Verse 21 says they “…returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch…” These were the towns where things got rough. They went back.

explanations.answer: Strengthen them and urge them to keep the faith
explanations.explanation: That's what verse 22 says. They were “…strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith.” They came back to those disciples with encouragement. That's good friends right there.

explanations.answer: Collect money for the church in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's a different kind of trip, and it isn't in this passage. Verse 22 says they were strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. No collection is mentioned here.

explanations.answer: Tell them to move somewhere much safer
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't tell anyone to pack up. Verse 22 says Paul and Barnabas were strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. Then they told them, “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God…”

That's the word. Verse 22 says, “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God…” They said it to the disciples they were encouraging. Paul and Barnabas had just lived hard days themselves.
Blessings would sound nicer, I'll admit. But verse 22 says, “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God…” The text names hardships, not blessings. It's honest talk.
These two had plenty of journeys, so I see the pick. But verse 22 says the disciples must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God. Hardships is the word Paul and Barnabas used.

Yes. Verse 23 says Paul and Barnabas “…appointed elders for them in each church…” So every church got leaders before the two moved on. Good baking, good teams, and no one left holding the oven mitts alone.
A building would be one way to go, but the text doesn't mention one. Verse 23 says Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church. They set up people, not a building.
The text doesn't say that. Verse 23 says Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church. They are called apostles in verse 14, but the new job here is elders.

That's right. Verse 23 says they appointed elders in each church, “…praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord, in whom they had believed.” So they prayed and they fasted while they appointed elders. They did it with the Lord in mind.

I can see why you'd skip that detail, but it's right there in verse 23. They appointed elders in each church, “…praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord, in whom they had believed.” So the answer is True. They fasted as they did it.
Yes, friend. Verse 25 says that when they had spoken the word in Perga, “…they went down to Attalia.” Verse 26 says they sailed from there to Antioch. Attalia is the last stop before the boat.
Caesarea is a good guess, but it isn't named in this passage. Verse 25 says that after Perga, they went down to Attalia. From Attalia they sailed to Antioch.
Troas is a real place too, but it's not here. Verse 25 says that after speaking the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia. It's the next stop on the way home.

explanations.answer: Report all that God had done through them
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 27 says they gathered the church together and “…reported all that God had done through them…” Notice who gets the credit. God did it through them.

explanations.answer: Ask the church to send a bigger team
explanations.explanation: Asking for a bigger team is how I'd go too, with all these cookie boxes to fill. But the text doesn't say it. Verse 27 says they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them. A report, not a request.

explanations.answer: Choose who goes on the next trip
explanations.explanation: Nothing about a next trip in this passage. Verse 27 says that when they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them. They came home to tell the story.
You got it. Verse 27 says God “…had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.” Gentiles means people who weren't Jews. God opened that door, and that's what Paul and Barnabas reported.
Samaritans are a good guess, but they aren't in this report. Verse 27 says God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. That's the word Paul and Barnabas used.
Levites aren't mentioned in this passage. Verse 27 says God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. Gentiles are people who aren't Jews, and that's who the door opened to.
